finding.claim: SQL injection in /search: the q parameter is interpolated into the SQL string with an f-string. An unauthenticated attacker can break out of the LIKE literal and run arbitrary SELECTs, for example a UNION to read any table in shop.db (users, credentials, orders, and so on). The same query also exposes the price and owner columns that the other routes treat as separate.
finding.sink: db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'") on the sqlite3 connection

trace.note: term = request.args.get('q', '') takes attacker-controlled input with no validation
term is formatted directly into the SQL text via an f-string, not bound as a parameter
query results are returned to the caller as JSON, so the injection is a direct data-exfiltration channel

finding.guards_checked: No authentication or authorization on the route. No input validation, escaping or length limit. No parameter binding here, unlike the other two routes (lines 18 and 25), which use '?' placeholders. No WAF or middleware in app.py. sqlite3 execute() rejects multiple statements, so stacked queries are blocked, but UNION-based and boolean/blind injection still work.

verdict.reason: app.py:11 reads q unvalidated and app.py:12 f-strings it into the LIKE literal with no auth, binding or allowlist, and app.py:13 returns the rows as JSON, so a UNION payload can read any table, while lines 18 and 25 use '?' binding and are safe.
